benchmarks.metaTitle: Average Test Scores: Reaction Time, CPS, Schulte and Memory
benchmarks.metaDescription: Real player averages: median reaction time 369 ms, 7 CPS, Schulte table 26.4 s, digit span 7. See full distributions, top 10% scores, and where your result lands.
benchmarks.title: Average Scores on Our Reflex, Focus and Memory Tests
benchmarks.intro: Medians, top scores and full distributions from more than 44,000 player results on FreeFocusGames. Each player counts once, with their best result. Take a test, then come back to see where you land.
benchmarks.methodLink: How we collect and filter this data

reactionTime.name: Reaction time
reactionTime.heading: Average reaction time
reactionTime.text: The median player averages 369 ms over five rounds. Under 284 ms puts you in the top 10%, and under 233 ms in the top 1%. Your device adds some delay, so online results run slower than lab figures.
reactionTime.aria: Histogram of best reaction time averages. Most players fall between 280 and 440 ms; the median is 369 ms.
reactionTime.note: Bars are 20 ms wide. 218 players between 800 and 1,000 ms are not shown.

tenSeconds.name: 10 Second Challenge
tenSeconds.heading: 10 Second Challenge: how close do people get?
tenSeconds.text: On their best try, half of players stop within 32 ms of 10 seconds. The top 10% are within 2 ms, and about 1 in 100 stop at exactly 10.000. These are results with the timer visible.
tenSeconds.aria: Bar chart of how far players stopped from 10 seconds. The largest group stopped within 10 ms.
tenSeconds.note: Bars are ranges, from under 10 ms to 1–3 seconds away.

schulte.name: Schulte table 5×5
schulte.heading: Average Schulte table time (5×5)
schulte.text: The median best time is 26.4 seconds, including a 2-second penalty for each wrong tap. Under 17.1 seconds puts you in the top 10%, and under 11.6 seconds in the top 1%.
schulte.aria: Histogram of best Schulte table times. Most players finish between 16 and 34 seconds; the median is 26.4 seconds.
schulte.note: Bars are 2 seconds wide. 267 players above 70 seconds are not shown.

cps.name: CPS test (5 s)
cps.heading: Average CPS (clicks per second)
cps.text: In the 5-second test, the median player reaches 7.0 clicks per second. 11 CPS puts you in the top 10%, and 14.4 in the top 1%. Results above 16 CPS are excluded as likely auto-clickers.
cps.aria: Histogram of best CPS scores. Most players reach 5 to 9 CPS; the median is 7.0.

digitSpan.name: Digit span (forward)
digitSpan.heading: Average digit span
digitSpan.text: Half of players recall at least 7 digits in order, matching the classic "seven, plus or minus two". The top 10% reach 10 digits or more. This is early data from 214 players.
digitSpan.aria: Bar chart of best forward digit spans. The most common span is 6 digits; the median is 7.
digitSpan.note: Each bar is one span length.

trailMaking.name: Trail Making Test
trailMaking.heading: Average Trail Making Test times
trailMaking.text: The median player finishes Part A in 34.6 seconds and Part B in 58.8 seconds. The top 10% are under 24.2 and 39.0 seconds. Medians and top 10% show Part A / Part B; the chart shows both parts combined. Early data from 201 players.
trailMaking.aria: Histogram of combined Trail Making Test times. Most players finish both parts in 70 to 110 seconds.
trailMaking.note: Bars are 10 seconds wide. 12 players above 200 seconds are not shown.

nback.heading: Dual n-back: how far do players get?
nback.text: 576 players have cleared dual n-back at 2-back or higher. Our leaderboard keeps each player's fastest clear rather than their highest level, so these shares are lower bounds.

items.q: What is a good reaction time?
items.a: On our test, under 300 ms is faster than about 84% of players, and the median is 369 ms.
The median in our 5-second CPS test is 7.0 clicks per second. Most players fall between 5 and 9.

items.q: Can I compare these with other sites, such as Human Benchmark?
items.a: Only roughly. Each site uses its own rules, number of rounds and players, and devices add different delays, so the same person can score differently on each.

items.q: Why use each player's best result?
items.a: The leaderboard keeps one best result per player, so every player counts once. Best results are a little faster than typical attempts.
